### **1.  Introduction & Executive Summary** 

##### **1.1 Introduction** 

Since the release of the last _3-Year Silver Forecast_ (on 27th June 2011), silver posted a brief rally before the price met a strong resistance at the $40/oz mark. Although silver has then strengthened again to reach a three-month high of over $43 at the time of writing, it has massively underperformed gold which is currently trading at a new all-time-high of $1,880.  This is a sharp contrast to early part of 2011 when silver was the leading metal in the commodity complex. 

Central to silver’s recent lacklustre performance is that developments on the macroeconomic front have substantially challenged the previously bullish view on silver and other industrial metals that were prevalent in early 2011.  Among these, the downgrade of the US credit rating and mounting concerns over sovereign debt in Europe took pride of place, which resulted in

investors selling riskier products and moving into haven assets such as gold. Related to this has also been increasing fears over a double dip recession in western economies, as almost all of economic statistics released have been well below market expectation. The US economy, for example, stumbled badly in the first half and came dangerously close to contracting in the first quarter. Weak growth data was also seen in the Eurozone’s main economies, Germany and France, which has put considerable pressure on European politicians working over ways to stop the debt crisis from engulfing Spain and Italy. Looking ahead, while some modest increase in the silver price is possible in the very short term, we would caution that the risk is to the downside in coming weeks. Concern about inflation will also continue to be at the forefront of investors’ minds, as many look at elevated energy and food prices as a lead indicator of future inflation or a weakening of the purchasing power of the dollar. 

As such, we would expect silver to bounce back towards $50 by the end of 2011, with the price averaging $38.75 for the full year under our **Base Case** .  It is important to point out that the eruption of recent sovereign debt crisis has raised the price in our Base Case towards levels once reserved for our most bullish variant, Scenario B.  This largely explains why we have trimmed the probability of this outcome from 50% at the time of our June report to 45% now.  However, while we do not rule out a breach of $50 later this year, we believe such levels are not sustainable.  Unlike gold where investment demand is more based on medium to long term views, investor interest in silver has been much more speculatively driven.  As such, investors could quickly liquidate their long positions if certain targets are achieved and therefore prices are vulnerable to any change in investor sentiment. 

Moving to 2012, we expect the aforementioned positive factors to remain broadly in place.  However, it may prove difficult to sustain investment and therefore prices, unless fresh supportive news emerges.  This could begin to threaten silver (and gold) prices as the year progresses, although the average for 2012 will continue to hit a new record of $40.40, due to higher starting point.  With more interest rate hikes and further fiscal tightening to take place in 2013, the slide back in prices could then accelerate, with the average price then falling to $28.90 in 2013. 

In addition to the Base Case, we also offer two alternative scenarios for the global economy that are very different to our central forecast.  In each instance, these have distinct implications for the level and trajectory of silver prices over 2011-13. 

**Scenario B** presents the most positive outlook for silver prices, with an investor led bull market continuing throughout the forecast period.  It is important to stress that we have raised the probability of this scenario from 30% to 40% since the previous report, reflecting the rapidly deteriorating sovereign debt situation on both sides of the Atlantic. A complete contrast is **Scenario C** , where investment will start to slip later this year. Given the greater likelihood of a continuation of loose fiscal and monetary policies in the United States, we assign this scenario a 15% probability, 5% lower than in June. Under this scenario, the weakness in the silver price is basis a secular recovery in the dollar and a low level of inflation, reflecting governments’ failure to boost private demand and consumer spending in advanced economies. The prolonged period of low inflation in western countries will also be compounded by further austerity measures and tighter monetary policy at a time when economic growth is still sluggish and unemployment rates remain high. These factors should reduce silver’s appeal to investors, most notably from 2012 onwards, when a marked reduction in investment results in prices slipping to levels that are more in line with silver’s underlying supply/demand fundamentals. **6** 3-Year Silver Forecast - August 2011 **CONFIDENTIAL** It is of note that the silver price under this scenario has been revised upward noticeably compared with our previous forecast. This reflects the resilient price performance seen since early July and a higher likely starting point for the silver price in forthcoming years. Much of the above has focused on the principal economic variables and investment. As mentioned

previously, however, we do not subscribe to the view that price direction and level are determined by investment alone.  The following analysis of expected trends in the underlying supply/demand variables shows that these will also play an important, if subsidiary, role in silver price determination in 2011-13. 

##### **1.2 Base Case Scenario** 

On the supply side, global **mine production** is expected to trend upwards from 2011 to 2013, posting successive record highs in each year.  Growth over 2011 and 2012 averages 6%, due to a robust project pipeline, which is bolstered by strong precious metals prices and a healthy performance by the base metals sector.  In 2013, the increase slows to 3%, primarily as reserves at a number of maturing operations begin to wane.  Nonetheless, output still reaches close to 870 Moz, over 115 Moz higher than produced in 2010. Since the previous forecast, output in 2012 and 2013 has been amended upwards, mostly in response to our higher expectations for silver prices; the outlook for 2011, however, remains unchanged, as prices are less able to exert an influence over the short term. 

**Scrap** supply, meanwhile, is forecast to take a different path.  After reaching a peak of 215 Moz in 2010, recycled silver volumes fall and then flatten in 2011 and 2012 respectively, before dropping below 200 Moz in 2013.  This trajectory is largely due to ongoing losses from the photographic sector, rising industrial scrap and price-led gains in 2011 and 2012 and steep losses in 2013 from jewellery and silverware.  The most notable change since the last forecast has been to supply in 2012, which has been adjusted significantly higher to reflect stronger jewellery scrap due to higher prices. 

With regard to **net producer hedging** , we expect some 55 Moz of supply from this source this year. Prolonged price strength in 2012 fosters another year of hedging, before lower prices decline in 2013 prompts a return to de-hedging.  The volumes of hedging this year and next have been revised notably upwards from the last report, although de-hedging has remained unchanged. **Net government sales** , meanwhile, 









post a steadily declining trajectory over 2011-2013, unaltered since the June forecast.  Such sales remain a small proportion of total supply, accounting for an average of just 1.4% over the forecast period. 

On the demand side, total fabrication is set to climb by over 10% from 2010 to 2013.  By far the largest component of this is **industrial** fabrication, which will reach successive record highs over the forecast.  The fastest rate of growth is seen this year, as the market goes through the final stages of recovery following the credit crunch.  Thereafter, demand posts further gains (albeit at a slower rate), leaving its total in 2013 almost 50 Moz higher than the 2011 level.  Since the last forecast, the series has been revised lower due to the downwards modification to GDP growth. 

**Jewellery** fabrication is

also forecast to rise over 2011-2013, despite climbing prices.  The reasons underpinning this trajectory remain unchanged since our last report, namely ongoing market penetration in the youth demographic and substitution gains at the expense of gold.  The marked boost in 2013 offtake is a result of the anticipated price fall, coupled with increased consumer spending. **Silverware** , meanwhile, will maintain its long term trend of decline over the next two years before enjoying by a modest price-led recovery in 2013, although the total remains historically low. **Photographic** demand continues to track lower, primarily as digital technology continues to erode halide technology’s share. 

Finally, surging demand for coins and medals is set to see a record high in 2011.  Although volumes will start to wane over 2012 and 2013, they remain elevated nonetheless according to historical standards. 

Overall, the supply and demand figures forecast show that the market will remain in surplus (as defined by the sum of mine production plus scrap less fabrication) over the next three years, which suggests that the silver price is vulnerable to a major correction. Nevertheless, given that the economic backdrop will remain generally favourable for investment demand for silver, we expect investors to comfortably absorb the surplus metal over the forecast period.

**Scenario B** traces the most bullish outcome for silver prices over the forecast period.  This price action occurs against a highly inflationary macroeconomic backdrop, which combined with dollar weakness

Higher prices trigger higher levels of supply from all sources, most notably scrap and net producer hedging. Despite more rapid declines in silverware and photography, fabrication demand in 2013 is still over 45 Moz higher than the Base Case. In contrast, coin demand has been lifted by 15 Moz in every year of the forecast, due to growing safe h

aven purchases. Elsewhere, we now forecast higher mine production and scrap supply, due to more robust price performance in 2012 and 2013. **Scenario C** , in contrast, presents the most bearish environment for silver prices. Under this economic variant, silver prices face three consecutive years of decline, posting an annual average of $21.95 by 2013, almost $7 lower than in our Base Case. This lacklustre performance is a result of sluggish economic growth, reflecting the failure of fiscal and monetary policies to stimulate consumption. Although this investor-led bear market does see a hefty decline in prices, the outcome would arguably be far worse, were it not for the support expected to emerge from other supply/demand developments. Total supply proves relatively restrained, due mainly to lower scrap coupled with a return to net producer de-hedging returns in 2012 (a year earlier than in the Base Case). With regard to fabrication demand, industrial offtake will post the smallest increase over the forecast than in the other scenarios, reflecting the slower rate of GDP growth. Coin offtake is also significantly weaker under this scenario, although jewellery and silverware will post stronger outcomes in light of weaker prices. Since the last report, the most notable revision has been a lift in coin fabrication to reflect surging demand for physical silver as a hedge. Even in emerging markets where growth has been fairly strong, continuing inflationary pressures on the back of a sharp rally in commodity prices has prompted authorities in a number of countries to tighten monetary policy further, also slowing the global economy. ##### **2.3 Base Case Scenario** Our forecast for **global economic growth** in 2011 has been revised lower since our last report. After a major rebound in 2010, world GDP growth is set to slow down this year to 2.7%, down slightly from 2.9% in our June forecast. This is due to the indebted nature of both governments and consumers in much of the developed world. Meanwhile, further tightening of monetary policies in emerging markets to fight surging inflation will also slow down world GDP growth this year. This is followed by marginally faster growth in 2012 and 2013 as the more traditional sources of growth, such as consumer spending and the property market, start to improve. The latter will be aided by unemployment beginning to slowly recede, albeit from elevated levels. **US** GDP grew at an annualised rate of 1.3% in the second quarter, well below the consensus range. In addition, GDP growth for the first quarter of 2011 had been revised sharply lower from 1.8% to 0.4%, highlighting the underlying weakness of the

US economy. The main reason for these disappointing figures was weak consumer spending, as this key driver of the US economy rose by a mere 0.1% from April to June this year. Meanwhile, it also reflects a continuation of an elevated unemployment rate coupled with a lacklustre property market, both of which are likely to remain in place for an extended period. While the Fed could start further unconventional policies to stimulate the economy, fiscal room is becoming extremely limited, particularly following the recent downgrade. Furthermore, increasing inflation pressure and requests for higher yield on its treasury bonds from developing countries will eventually see the Fed tighten its policy in late 2012. This combined with the waning support from fiscal policy will certainly restrict annual GDP growth to 2.0% in both 2012 and 2013. Our GDP forecast for **EU-27** series has been revised lower since the previous forecast, as growth in Germany and France, the two largest economies in Europe, both stalled in the second quarter. In our view, this sharp deceleration in Europe’s major economies will not only hit the overall eurozone growth this year but also threatens to complicate the challenge facing the region’s policy makers as they seek to combat the escalating debt crisis. Therefore, average EU growth will be around 1.3% in 2011. Given the excessive level of public debt in many European countries, we would expect further austerity measures to take place in a regional number of southern European countries over the next two years, which in turn will continue to drag down the region’s growth. As such, we continue to expect only modest GDP growth in 2012 and 2013 as its economies gradually recover. **Japan** ’s economy has recovered faster than expected from the aftermath of the earthquake and tsunami. Factory output grew by 3.9% in June, as supply chain concerns eased while household spending gradually improved. As such, we have raised our forecast for Japanese GDP growth slightly to 0.9% this year. While manufacturers have been able to overcome various challenges including a shortage of electricity, other factors continue to remain a threat, particularly in terms of a stronger Japanese yen; due to the ongoing debt issues in the United States and Europe, the yen rose to record highs against the dollar in late July, which put further pressure on the export sector. Some support for silver demand is expected to come from substitution from gold (due its substantial price gains), although much of the downshift should be to branded, gemset silver, which will do much to lift the value of sales but less so the fine weight.  Emerging markets’ robust GDP growth should also assist, but a negative reaction to the price in India should counter these.  Since the June report, demand figures have been trimmed for all the three years mainly in light of the upward price revisions. 

Under **Scenario C** , demand growth accelerates in each year of the forecast as prices materially weaken from 2012 onwards, with the result that demand in that year overtakes Scenario B.  This is mainly as the benefits of these lower prices offset slower GDP growth.  By 2013, offtake reaches a level a shade under 200 Moz, a new record high.  Since the last report, there have been some minor changes, in that demand in 2011 and 2012 has been trimmed slightly due to higher prices and lower GDP growth. 

##### **9.2 Silverware** 

###### **9.2.1  Introduction** 

Silverware demand has suffered from long term structural changes, with global consumption of 50.3 Moz last year almost 60% below the 1997 peak.  Although some drivers of the decline were technological, such as the introduction of stainless steel, of much greater importance has been the impact of societal changes in India and the western world. 

In India, demand was historically investment-focused as silverware was viewed by many as a relatively simple and reliable store of wealth.  However, over the last decade, consumers have looked to bars and coins as more trustworthy vehicles, as undercarating by traders had led to a lack of consumer confidence in non-regulated items.  In the west, losses were mainly due to a move away from formal entertaining and from the gifting of silverware at weddings or other events. The rise in the silver price over the last few

years has also contributed as it encouraged a shift from solid to plated items. ###### **9.2.2 Base Case Scenario** We expect the developing world to stay susceptible to price volatility, while in the western world, weaker consumer sentiment (as economies remain unstable) is likely to translate into demand losses, with this combination driving global offtake down by 8% this year. Higher prices remain the chief culprit for further losses in 2012 (falling a further 5% year-on-year) before a sharp correction in the silver price in 2013 brings with it a recovery in demand from the developing world; modest gains in India and south-east Asian markets should offset further weakness within Europe and North America. However, that year’s 7% rise still leaves the global number 6% below the 2010 figure. Our 2011 silverware figure has been revised slightly lower than in our June publication, with higher silver prices and a weaker than anticipated economic climate necessitating this change. ###### **9.2.3 Alternative Scenarios** The greatest losses are forecast under **Scenario B** , where higher silver prices are expected to drive global consumption down heavily in each of the forecast years, culminating in a fall of over 20% in 2013 as silver surpasses $60/oz. This translates into a loss of over 20 Moz from 2010 to 2013, with all regions and India in particular suffering heavy losses. The lift to our price forecasts since June has also led to most countries’ demand estimates, especially for India, being trimmed. Under **Scenario C** , demand is expected to retreat by just 4% in 2011, with a slightly stronger Indian market partially offsetting falls elsewhere. Growth returns in 2012 at a modest 1%, as prices ease, and then improves to 5% in 2013.
